title: Ezekiel 10 — The kavod departs the temple

paragraphs.text: וָאֶרְאֶ֗ה וְהִנֵּ֤ה אֶל־הָרָקִ֙יעַ֙ אֲשֶׁר֙ עַל־רֹ֣אשׁ הַכְּרֻבִ֔ים כְּאֶ֣בֶן סַפִּ֔יר כְּמַרְאֵ֖ה דְּמ֣וּת כִּסֵּ֑א נִרְאָ֖ה עֲלֵיהֶֽם׃

i18n.en: I looked, and behold — above the dome that was over the heads of the cherubim, like sapphire stone, like the appearance of the likeness of a throne, was seen above them.

paragraphs.commentary: **The chapter opens by recalling the throne-vision of chapter 1.** Five distinct elements link this verse to 1:22-26: (1) *ha-raqia* — the dome — same Hebrew word, same position above the figures' heads; (2) *al-rosh ha-keruvim* — *over the heads of the cherubim* — the chapter's first naming of the figures as *cherubim*; (3) *k'eben sappir* — *like sapphire stone* — the throne-platform material of 1:26 (and the Sinai theophany of Ex 24:10); (4) *kemar'eh demut kisse* — *like the appearance of the likeness of a throne* — the hedging formula of 1:26 verbatim; (5) *nir'ah aleihem* — *was seen above them* — the throne-position relative to the chayyot/cherubim. // The verse establishes the chapter's structural claim: *this is the same vision as chapter 1*. Where chapter 1 named the figures *chayyot*, chapter 10 names them *keruvim* — the explicit identification will land at v15, v20, v22. The chapter's keystone is precisely this identification: Ezekiel's chayyot ARE the cherubim, the ANE-iconographic winged composite throne-attendants that flank the Ark (Ex 25:18-20) and guard the way to the Tree of Life (Gen 3:24).

paragraphs.text: וַיֹּ֜אמֶר אֶל־הָאִ֣ישׁ ׀ לְבֻ֣שׁ הַבַּדִּ֗ים וַיֹּ֡אמֶר בֹּא֩ אֶל־בֵּינ֨וֹת לַגַּלְגַּ֜ל אֶל־תַּ֣חַת לַכְּר֗וּב וּמַלֵּ֨א חָפְנֶ֤יךָ גַֽחֲלֵי־אֵשׁ֙ מִבֵּינ֣וֹת לַכְּרֻבִ֔ים וּזְרֹ֖ק עַל־הָעִ֑יר וַיָּבֹ֖א לְעֵינָֽי׃

i18n.en: He said to the man clothed in linen: "Come into the midst of the *galgal*, under the cherub, and fill your two handfuls with coals of fire from between the cherubim, and scatter them over the city." And he went in before my eyes.

paragraphs.commentary: **A new figure enters: *ha-ish levush ha-badim* — the man clothed in linen.** *Badim* (בַּדִּים) is the Hebrew term for linen-cloth as worn by priests in cultic contexts (Lev 6:10, 16:4 of the high priest on Yom Kippur). The same figure appears in Dan 10:5, 12:6-7 (the man clothed in linen by the Tigris). The Christian tradition identifies him as an angelic figure; the Hebrew gives him no name. The chapter's narrative pivots on his action: he is to take fire from the apparatus and scatter it over the city as judgment. // ***Galgal*** (גַּלְגַּל) — *the wheel-rim, the rolling-thing*. This is the chapter's distinctive vocabulary contribution: the wheels (*ofanim*) of chapter 1 are now called *galgal*. The relationship between *ofan* and *galgal* is explained in v13 — *galgal* is what the wheels are called *in his hearing* (i.e., what the heavenly attendants call them). The two terms refer to the same object; the chapter is documenting the alternative technical name. *Galgal* later becomes the standard term for the throne-wheel in Jewish mystical tradition (Hekhalot literature, *Shi'ur Qomah*) and is a load-bearing word in the *Merkavah* (chariot) mystical-tradition.

paragraphs.text: וְהַכְּרֻבִ֗ים עֹֽמְדִ֛ים מִימִ֥ין לַבַּ֖יִת בְּבֹא֣וֹ הָאִ֑ישׁ וְהֶעָנָ֣ן מָלֵ֔א אֶת־הֶחָצֵ֖ר הַפְּנִימִֽית׃

i18n.en: The cherubim were standing on the right side of the house when the man came in; and the cloud filled the inner court.

paragraphs.commentary: **The cloud fills the inner court.** *He-anan male et he-chatzer ha-penimit* — *the cloud filled the inner court*. The cloud-filling-the-house motif recurs across the Hebrew Bible's most-charged divine-presence moments: Ex 40:34-35 (the cloud filled the Tabernacle and Moses could not enter), 1 Kgs 8:10-11 / 2 Chr 5:13-14 (the cloud filled the Temple at Solomon's dedication and the priests could not stand to minister). The chapter is reusing the canonical cloud-filling-the-temple vocabulary — but now in the **reverse direction**: where the cloud-filling-temple in Exodus and Kings was *arrival* (the kavod taking up residence), the cloud-filling here is part of the *departure* sequence the chapter narrates. The chapter is doing the Exodus-presence-arrival in reverse.

paragraphs.text: וַיָּ֤רָם כְּבוֹד־יְהוָה֙ מֵעַ֣ל הַכְּר֔וּב עַ֖ל מִפְתַּ֣ן הַבָּ֑יִת וַיִּמָּלֵ֤א הַבַּ֙יִת֙ אֶת־הֶ֣עָנָ֔ן וְהֶֽחָצֵר֙ מָֽלְאָ֔ה אֶת־נֹ֖גַהּ כְּב֥וֹד יְהוָֽה׃

i18n.en: The glory of YHWH rose up from above the cherub onto the threshold of the house; the house was filled with the cloud, and the court was filled with the brightness of the glory of YHWH.

paragraphs.commentary: **The first stage of the departure.** *Vayyaram kvod-YHWH me-al ha-keruv al miftan ha-bayit* — *the kavod-YHWH rose up from above the cherub onto the threshold of the house*. The departure-motion is staged in two stages: from above-the-cherub (the throne-position of ch 1:26 / 10:1) → onto the threshold of the temple. The threshold (*miftan*) is the architectural transition-point between inside and outside; the chapter is staging the kavod's progress *toward the door*. // *Nogah kvod YHWH* — *the brightness of the glory of YHWH* — recapitulates the radiance vocabulary of ch 1:4, 13, 27, 28 (*nogah lo saviv* — *brightness around him*). The presence is luminous, not merely conceptual. // The chapter is one of the Hebrew Bible's most-cited theological-textual passages on the *divine abandonment* of the Temple. Read from the prophetic-historical standpoint: Jerusalem is being abandoned ahead of its 587/586 BCE destruction; the *kavod* leaves before the Babylonians arrive. The chapter is the textual record of the divine presence withdrawing before the human catastrophe.

paragraphs.text: וְקוֹל֙ כַּנְפֵ֣י הַכְּרוּבִ֔ים נִשְׁמַ֕ע עַד־הֶחָצֵ֖ר הַחִיצֹנָ֑ה כְּק֥וֹל אֵל־שַׁדַּ֖י בְּדַבְּרֽוֹ׃

i18n.en: The sound of the cherubim's wings was heard as far as the outer court — like the voice of El-Shaddai when he speaks.

paragraphs.commentary: **The wing-sound recapitulates 1:24.** Ezek 1:24 stacked four similes for the wing-sound: many waters, voice of Shaddai, tumultuous sound, voice of an army. Ezek 10:5 cites only one — *qol El-Shaddai b'dabro* — *the voice of El-Shaddai when he speaks*. The chapter is selecting the chapter-1 simile that fits the *speaking* register: the cherubim are now in motion, and the sound their wings make is the *speaking* register of the divine voice. // *El-Shaddai* (אֵל שַׁדַּי) is the patriarchal divine name (see glossary entry `qol-mayim-rabbim` for the etymology and the preservation policy). The chapter does not use the alternative *qol mayim rabbim* (sound of many waters) of ch 1:24 — it picks the voice-register specifically.

paragraphs.text: וַיְהִ֗י בְּצַוֺּתוֹ֙ אֶת־הָאִ֤ישׁ לְבֻֽשׁ־הַבַּדִּים֙ לֵאמֹ֔ר קַ֥ח אֵשׁ֙ מִבֵּינ֣וֹת לַגַּלְגַּ֔ל מִבֵּינ֖וֹת לַכְּרוּבִ֑ים וַיָּבֹא֙ וַֽיַּעֲמֹ֔ד אֵ֖צֶל הָאוֹפָֽן׃

i18n.en: When he commanded the man clothed in linen, saying, "Take fire from between the *galgal*, from between the cherubim," the man came and stood beside the wheel.

paragraphs.commentary: **The chapter uses both *galgal* and *ofan* in the same verse.** *Mi-beinot la-galgal* — *from between the galgal*. *Etzel ha-ofan* — *beside the wheel*. The two terms are the chapter's twin technical names for the same object, used interchangeably. *Galgal* is the chapter's distinctive vocabulary; *ofan* carries over from chapter 1. The man-clothed-in-linen takes his position *beside* the wheel-system to receive the fire.

paragraphs.text: וַיִּשְׁלַח֩ הַכְּר֨וּב אֶת־יָד֜וֹ מִבֵּינ֣וֹת לַכְּרוּבִ֗ים אֶל־הָאֵשׁ֙ אֲשֶׁר֙ בֵּינ֣וֹת הַכְּרֻבִ֔ים וַיִּשָּׂא֙ וַיִּתֵּ֔ן אֶל־חָפְנֵ֖י לְבֻ֣שׁ הַבַּדִּ֑ים וַיִּקַּ֖ח וַיֵּצֵֽא׃

i18n.en: The cherub reached out his hand from between the cherubim to the fire that was between the cherubim; he lifted it and put it into the two handfuls of the one clothed in linen, who took it and went out.

paragraphs.commentary: **The fire-transfer.** A single cherub reaches into the fire-source and hands it to the man clothed in linen — a precise transfer-action. The Hebrew preserves the awkwardness of describing one cherub's hand among many cherubim (*ha-keruv... mi-beinot ha-keruvim... el-ha-esh asher beinot ha-keruvim*) — the chapter is meticulous about the spatial choreography. // The fire from between the cherubim is the same fire-source as the chayyot's burning coals in 1:13 (*gachalei esh*). The same combustion / discharge phenomenon is being redeployed for the city-judgment action of v2.

paragraphs.text: וַיֵּרָ֖א לַכְּרֻבִ֑ים תַּבְנִית֙ יַד־אָדָ֔ם תַּ֖חַת כַּנְפֵיהֶֽם׃

i18n.en: There was seen on the cherubim the pattern of a human hand under their wings.

paragraphs.commentary: **The human-hand-under-the-wings detail recapitulates 1:8.** Same anatomical observation, same wording (*yad adam tachat kanfeihem*). The chapter is verbally citing the chapter-1 figure-description, preparing the reader for the identification of v15.

paragraphs.text: וָאֶרְאֶ֗ה וְהִנֵּ֨ה אַרְבָּעָ֣ה אוֹפַנִּים֮ אֵ֣צֶל הַכְּרוּבִים֒ אוֹפַ֣ן אֶחָ֗ד אֵ֚צֶל הַכְּר֣וּב אֶחָ֔ד וְאוֹפַ֣ן אֶחָ֔ד אֵ֖צֶל הַכְּר֣וּב אֶחָ֑ד וּמַרְאֵה֙ הָא֣וֹפַנִּ֔ים כְּעֵ֖ין אֶ֥בֶן תַּרְשִֽׁישׁ׃

i18n.en: I looked, and behold — four wheels beside the cherubim, one wheel beside one cherub, and one wheel beside one cherub; and the appearance of the wheels was like the look of tarshish-stone.

paragraphs.commentary: **Recapitulation of 1:15-16.** *Arba'ah ofannim etzel ha-keruvim* — *four wheels beside the cherubim*. Same one-wheel-per-cherub configuration as ch 1. Same *tarshish-stone* descriptor of the wheel material (golden-yellow gemstone, see glossary entry `tarshish-stone`). The chapter is methodically re-describing the apparatus to leave no doubt about its identity with ch 1.

paragraphs.text: וּמַ֨רְאֵיהֶ֔ם דְּמ֥וּת אֶחָ֖ד לְאַרְבַּעְתָּ֑ם כַּאֲשֶׁ֛ר יִהְיֶ֥ה הָאוֹפַ֖ן בְּת֥וֹךְ הָאוֹפָֽן׃

i18n.en: Their appearance — the four of them had one likeness — was as if a wheel were within a wheel.

paragraphs.commentary: **The wheel-within-wheel verbatim from 1:16.** Same Hebrew construction, same hedging formula (*ka-asher yihyeh* — *as if it would be*). The chapter is doing structural citation of chapter 1 — each verse of 10:9-12 maps to a verse in 1:15-18, with the same details, sometimes the same exact wording. The textual identity of the two visions is being established by verbal repetition.

paragraphs.text: בְּלֶכְתָּ֗ם אֶל־אַרְבַּ֤עַת רִבְעֵיהֶם֙ יֵלֵ֔כוּ לֹ֥א יִסַּ֖בּוּ בְּלֶכְתָּ֑ם כִּ֣י הַמָּק֞וֹם אֲשֶׁר־יִפְנֶ֤ה הָרֹאשׁ֙ אַחֲרָ֣יו יֵלֵ֔כוּ לֹ֥א יִסַּ֖בּוּ בְּלֶכְתָּֽם׃

i18n.en: When they went, they went on their four sides; they did not turn as they went. Toward the place where the head turned, after it they would go; they did not turn as they went.

paragraphs.commentary: **The no-turning motion recapitulated from 1:9, 1:12, 1:17.** New detail: *ha-makom asher yifneh ha-rosh acharav yelekhu* — *toward the place where the head turned, after it they would go*. The chapter clarifies the directional logic — the system follows where the *rosh* (head) turns. Whether *rosh* refers to the lead cherub, the throne-figure above, or an internal compass-mechanism is left unspecified.

paragraphs.text: וְכָל־בְּשָׂרָם֙ וְגַבֵּהֶ֔ם וִֽידֵיהֶ֖ם וְכַנְפֵיהֶ֑ם וְהָאֽוֹפַנִּ֗ים מְלֵאִ֤ים עֵינַ֙יִם֙ סָבִ֔יב לְאַרְבַּעְתָּ֖ם אוֹפַנֵּיהֶֽם׃

i18n.en: And all their flesh, their rims, their hands, their wings, and the wheels were full of eyes round about — for the four of them, their wheels.

paragraphs.commentary: **The eyes are now everywhere.** Where 1:18 placed eyes specifically on the wheel-rims (*gabbotam meleot einayim* — *their rims full of eyes*), 10:12 distributes them across the whole apparatus: *flesh, rims, hands, wings, and wheels*. The chapter is extending the eye-motif from the wheels to the cherubim themselves. The cherubim are now described as eye-covered creatures. // The textual move foreshadows Revelation 4:6, 4:8 — the four *zoa* (living creatures) of John's vision *are full of eyes around and within*, with the eye-motif transferred fully to the chayyot/cherubim themselves. The lens reading is consistent across the chapter: the perceptive-data-gathering surface of the apparatus is comprehensive.

paragraphs.text: לָא֖וֹפַנִּ֑ים לָהֶ֛ם קוֹרָ֥א הַגַּלְגַּ֖ל בְּאָזְנָֽי׃

i18n.en: As for the wheels — they were called *galgal* in my hearing.

paragraphs.commentary: **The chapter's most distinctive vocabulary moment.** The verse names the wheels' alternative technical term explicitly: *la-ofannim lahem qora ha-galgal b'aznai* — *as for the wheels, they were called galgal in my hearing*. The chapter is documenting that what the prophet heard the heavenly attendants call the wheels was *galgal*, not *ofan*. // *Galgal* (גַּלְגַּל) — from the root *gll* (to roll). The noun's lexical core is *rolling thing, wheel-rim, whirlwind*. It appears in the Hebrew Bible at Ps 77:18 (the *qol galgal* — *sound of rolling-thing*, a thunder-storm image), Isa 17:13 (whirling chaff), and Eccl 12:6 (the wheel at the well). // The verse becomes the foundational Hebrew Bible word for the rabbinic-mystical *Merkavah* (chariot) tradition. The *galgalim* of Ezekiel are the Hekhalot-literature *galgalim* — the throne-wheel layer of the multi-tiered heavenly throne. This single verse names what would become a load-bearing concept of Jewish mystical theology for the next two millennia.

paragraphs.text: וְאַרְבָּעָ֥ה פָנִ֖ים לְאֶחָ֑ד פְּנֵ֨י הָאֶחָ֜ד פְּנֵ֣י הַכְּר֗וּב וּפְנֵ֤י הַשֵּׁנִי֙ פְּנֵ֣י אָדָ֔ם וְהַשְּׁלִישִׁי֙ פְּנֵ֣י אַרְיֵ֔ה וְהָרְבִיעִ֖י פְּנֵי־נָֽשֶׁר׃

i18n.en: Each had four faces: the face of the first was the face of a cherub; the face of the second, the face of human; the third, the face of a lion; the fourth, the face of an eagle.

paragraphs.commentary: **The face-list differs from chapter 1.** Ch 1:10 listed: human, lion, ox, eagle. Ch 10:14 lists: cherub, human, lion, eagle — with the **cherub-face replacing the ox-face**. // The textual variation has been read in multiple ways: (1) a scribal corruption (the cherub-face is a copyist error for ox); (2) a deliberate development within the book (chapter 10 revising or supplementing chapter 1); (3) an internal reference (the cherub-face IS what an ox-face looks like to Ezekiel after the Kebar vision — the four-face creatures had ox-faces, and now seeing them again Ezekiel calls those faces *cherub-faces*); (4) the LXX of Ezek 1:10 actually reads cherub for ox at one position, suggesting the textual tradition is unstable. // The chapter does not resolve. The WoH translation preserves the Masoretic Text reading and surfaces the textual question in commentary. The verse is a known crux.

paragraphs.text: וַיֵּרֹ֖מּוּ הַכְּרוּבִ֑ים הִ֣יא הַחַיָּ֔ה אֲשֶׁ֥ר רָאִ֖יתִי בִּֽנְהַר־כְּבָֽר׃

i18n.en: The cherubim rose up — she is the living creature that I saw at the river Kebar.

paragraphs.commentary: **The chapter's keystone identification.** *Hi ha-chayyah asher ra'iti bi-nehar-Kevar* — *she is the chayyah (living creature) that I saw at the river Kebar*. The verse explicitly identifies the cherubim of chapter 10 with the chayyot of chapter 1. // Two grammatical features. First, *hi* — *she* — is feminine singular, referring back to *chayyah* (the singular collective noun used in 1:20-21 — *ruach ha-chayyah ba-ofannim* — *the ruach of the chayyah was in the wheels*). The four creatures are the chayyah grammatically singular, the cherubim grammatically plural — the chapter is using both registers. Second, *nehar Kevar* — *the river Kebar* — points back to 1:1, 1:3, anchoring the identification by geographic citation. // The verse is THE textual datum for any reading of Ezekiel's vision: chayyot AND cherubim are the same figures. The standard scholarly consensus (Greenberg, Block, Zimmerli) accepts this verbal identification; the chapter is not making a comparative-mythological move but a *direct identification*. // The Wheel of Heaven lens reads the identification as the chapter's most important contribution to the canon: the heavenly attendants of the throne — the canonical cherubim of Eden (Gen 3:24) and the Ark (Ex 25:18-20) — are the *chayyot* of the Kebar-canal vision. The figures Ezekiel saw moving with the technical apparatus are the same figures that flanked the Tree of Life and the Mercy Seat.

paragraphs.text: וּבְלֶ֙כֶת֙ הַכְּרוּבִ֔ים יֵלְכ֥וּ הָאוֹפַנִּ֖ים אֶצְלָ֑ם וּבִשְׂאֵ֨ת הַכְּרוּבִ֤ים אֶת־כַּנְפֵיהֶם֙ לָר֣וּם מֵעַ֣ל הָאָ֔רֶץ לֹא־יִסַּ֧בּוּ הָאוֹפַנִּ֛ים גַּם־הֵ֖ם מֵאֶצְלָֽם׃

i18n.en: When the cherubim went, the wheels went beside them; and when the cherubim lifted up their wings to rise from the land, the wheels too would not turn from beside them.

paragraphs.commentary: **Verbatim re-description of 1:19-21.** Same mechanical coupling between cherubim and wheels, same airborne capacity. The chapter is making sure no reader can mistake the apparatus for anything other than the chapter-1 system.

paragraphs.text: בְּעָמְדָ֣ם יַעֲמֹ֔דוּ וּבְרוֹמָ֖ם יֵר֣וֹמּוּ אוֹתָ֑ם כִּ֛י ר֥וּחַ הַחַיָּ֖ה בָּהֶֽם׃

i18n.en: When they stood, these would stand; when they rose up, these would rise up with them — for the *ruach* of the living creature was in them.

paragraphs.commentary: **The ruach-of-the-chayyah claim recapitulated from 1:20-21.** The same animating-directive principle named in chapter 1 is reaffirmed here for the wheel-cherubim system. The chapter is restating the unified-control-architecture claim verbatim. The integrated apparatus reading from chapter 1 carries over without modification.

paragraphs.text: וַיֵּצֵא֙ כְּב֣וֹד יְהוָ֔ה מֵעַ֖ל מִפְתַּ֣ן הַבָּ֑יִת וַֽיַּעֲמֹ֖ד עַל־הַכְּרוּבִֽים׃

i18n.en: The glory of YHWH went out from above the threshold of the house and stood above the cherubim.

paragraphs.commentary: **The second stage of the departure.** *Vayyetze kvod-YHWH me-al miftan ha-bayit* — *the kavod-YHWH went out from above the threshold of the house*. *Vayya'amod al ha-keruvim* — *and stood above the cherubim*. // The chapter is staging the departure in three stages: v4 (above cherub → onto threshold), v18 (off threshold → above cherubim again), v19 (cherubim lift up and depart). The kavod relocates from the inside of the Temple to the moving apparatus and then leaves with the apparatus. // The chapter is dramatizing the loss of the Temple's status as the locus of the divine presence. The kavod has moved out — onto the moving apparatus that will exit through the east gate (v19). The lens reads this as the divine-presence-apparatus making a controlled withdrawal.

paragraphs.text: וַיִּשְׂא֣וּ הַכְּרוּבִ֣ים אֶת־כַּ֠נְפֵיהֶם וַיֵּר֨וֹמּוּ מִן־הָאָ֤רֶץ לְעֵינַי֙ בְּצֵאתָ֔ם וְהָאֽוֹפַנִּ֖ים לְעֻמָּתָ֑ם וַֽיַּעֲמֹ֗ד פֶּ֣תַח שַׁ֤עַר בֵּית־יְהוָה֙ הַקַּדְמוֹנִ֔י וּכְב֧וֹד אֱלֹהֵֽי־יִשְׂרָאֵ֛ל עֲלֵיהֶ֖ם מִלְמָֽעְלָה׃

i18n.en: The cherubim lifted up their wings and rose from the land before my eyes as they went out — and the wheels were beside them. It stood at the entrance of the east gate of the house of YHWH, and the glory of the Elohim of Israel was above them from above.

paragraphs.commentary: **The third and decisive stage: the kavod exits.** The cherubim lift their wings, rise from the ground, and exit through the east gate of the Temple. The east gate (*sha'ar bet-YHWH ha-qadmoni*) faces sunrise — the standard ANE temple orientation, with the divine presence entering and exiting eastward. Ezek 11:23 will note the kavod's next position: above the Mount of Olives (east of Jerusalem). The chapter is staging the kavod's exit step by step: from temple interior → threshold → apparatus → above the apparatus → east gate → above the mountain east of the city. // *Kvod Elohei-Yisrael* — *the glory of the Elohim of Israel*. The verse uses the compound name *Elohei-Yisrael* — the same form as Genesis 33:20 (Jacob's altar *El-Elohei-Yisrael*), Ex 24:10 (the elders see Elohei-Yisrael at Sinai), Josh 7:13, 1 Sam 23:10-11. The chapter is invoking the patriarchal-Sinaitic divine name precisely at the moment of departure — the *kavod of the Elohim of Israel* (not just the kavod of YHWH) leaves the Temple. The covenantal name is being invoked at the covenantal-undoing moment.

paragraphs.text: הִ֣יא הַחַיָּ֗ה אֲשֶׁ֥ר רָאִ֛יתִי תַּ֥חַת אֱלֹהֵֽי־יִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל בִּֽנְהַר־כְּבָ֑ר וָאֵדַ֕ע כִּ֥י כְרוּבִ֖ים הֵֽמָּה׃

i18n.en: She is the living creature that I saw under the Elohim of Israel at the river Kebar — and I knew that they were cherubim.

paragraphs.commentary: ***Va-eda ki keruvim hemmah*** — *and I knew that they were cherubim*. The prophet's first-person recognition: he NOW knows what he saw at Kebar was *cherubim*. Chapter 1 did not name the figures; it called them *chayyot* (living creatures). Chapter 10 closes that gap by Ezekiel himself identifying the chayyot as cherubim. // The verse-formula is again the chapter's signature identification: *hi ha-chayyah* (singular collective) *asher ra'iti tachat Elohei-Yisrael bi-nehar-Kevar* — *she is the chayyah I saw under the Elohim of Israel at the river Kebar*. The compound divine name *Elohei-Yisrael* is reused (cf. v19), now in the explicit Kebar-recall. The patriarchal/covenantal name and the Kebar location anchor the identification. // The lens reads this verse as the chapter's interpretive payoff: the chayyot of ch1 — the apparatus, the technical-mechanical system — are the *cherubim*, the canonical Hebrew Bible attendants of the Throne and guardians of the Tree of Life. The chapter is bridging the technical and the iconographic registers. Ezekiel's vision is being absorbed into the existing canonical vocabulary of divine-presence attendants.

paragraphs.text: אַרְבָּעָ֨ה אַרְבָּעָ֤ה פָנִים֙ לְאֶחָ֔ד וְאַרְבַּ֥ע כְּנָפַ֖יִם לְאֶחָ֑ד וּדְמוּת֙ יְדֵ֣י אָדָ֔ם תַּ֖חַת כַּנְפֵיהֶֽם׃

i18n.en: Each had four faces, each had four wings, and the likeness of human hands was under their wings.

paragraphs.commentary: **The closing recap.** The verse summarizes the cherubim's design — four faces, four wings, human hands under wings — exactly as ch 1:6, 1:8 described the chayyot. The chapter ends with the identification fully cemented.

paragraphs.text: וּדְמ֣וּת פְּנֵיהֶ֔ם הֵ֣מָּה הַפָּנִ֗ים אֲשֶׁ֤ר רָאִ֙יתִי֙ עַל־נְהַר־כְּבָ֔ר מַרְאֵיהֶ֖ם וְאוֹתָ֑ם אִ֛ישׁ אֶל־עֵ֥בֶר פָּנָ֖יו יֵלֵֽכוּ׃

i18n.en: The likeness of their faces — these were the faces that I saw at the river Kebar, their appearance and themselves. Each would go in the direction of its face.

paragraphs.commentary: **Final restatement of the identification.** *Hemmah ha-panim asher ra'iti al-nehar-Kevar* — *these were the faces I saw at the river Kebar*. The chapter closes with the third Kebar-reference (v15, v20, v22) — every reference made by Ezekiel-in-first-person, all three serving the same identifying function. The Kebar-faces of chapter 1 are the cherub-faces of chapter 10. The vision has been brought into canonical-iconographic register. // *Ish el-ever panav yelekhu* — *each would go in the direction of its face* — the verbatim closing-detail of 1:9, 1:12. The chapter closes on the same mechanical observation that closed the figure-description in ch 1. The departure-narrative is complete; the apparatus has left the Temple; the kavod has gone east. The next chapter (Ezek 11) will pick up the departure at its next stopping-point: above the Mount of Olives, east of the city, where the kavod will rest before going into exile with the exiled community.
